                                                PROJECT NO. 58482

 LARGE LOAD DEMAND                                     §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 MANAGEMENT SERVICE                                    §
                                                       §                OF TEXAS

                   ELECTRIC RELIABILITY COUNCIL OF TEXAS, INC.’S
                   COMMENTS ON THE PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION

       Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. (ERCOT) files these comments to address the

Proposal for Publication (PFP) issued on July 30, 2026 by the Public Utility Commission of Texas

(Commission).1 The PFP proposes to add new rule 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) § 25.521

to implement the new Large Load Demand Management Service (LLDMS) established by Public

Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) § 39.170, 2 as enacted by Senate Bill 6 passed during Texas’s 89th

legislative session (S.B. 6).3 The deadline to file comments on the PFP is September 4, 2026. 4

These comments are therefore timely filed. An executive summary of these comments and a

comprehensive redline draft of ERCOT’s proposals are included at the end of this filing.

                   I.          RESPONSE TO QUESTIONS FOR COMMENTS

       Four questions for comment were included with the PFP. In addition, at the July 30, 2026

Open Meeting on the proposed PFP, Commissioner Hjaltman asked whether a qualified large load

customer should be permitted to divide its demand response capacity into separate megawatt (MW)

components and offer some MW into LLDMS while offering other MW into some other demand

response program. ERCOT offers the following comments on the Commission’s questions.

 A.     Should a large load customer that is available but not ultimately instructed to deploy
       during the LLDMS obligation period be compensated some percentage of the market
       clearing price for the large load customer’s availability to reduce demand during the
       LLDMS obligation period? If so, what is an appropriate payment to the large load
       customer for their availability during the LLDMS obligation period?

       ERCOT believes it is appropriate to compensate large load customers participating in

LLDMS for being available to deploy during the LLDMS obligation period (as confirmed by

verification testing), recognizing there are operational costs associated with maintaining

availability and that participating large load customers will forego the ability to participate in any

other Ancillary Services or demand response/reliability programs during the obligation period.

       If ERCOT were to procure LLDMS on a monthly or other longer-term basis, however, it

is concerned that the PFP’s proposed availability payment structure may make LLDMS

excessively costly and/or significantly limit the amount of LLDMS ERCOT can procure within

the available budget. For example, if, under a monthly procurement model, ERCOT determined

the month of December is a high-risk period but is unable to pinpoint when in December the

service would be deployed, ERCOT would need to assume for procurement purposes that

deployment payments (100% of the clearing price5) would be made for all hours of the monthly

obligation period (31 days or 744 hours), and the service clears at the current offer cap ($5,000 per

megawatt hour (MWh)).6 This means ERCOT would need to assume potential procurement costs

of up to $3.72 million/MWh ($5,000/MWh offer cap * 744-hour obligation period), which would

allow ERCOT procure only 14.5 MW of LLDMS to ensure it stays within budget ($54 million

budget / $3.72 million/MWh clearing price). And ultimately, under this hypothetical, ERCOT

could end up paying $930,000/MWh in availability costs for a service that is never needed to

deploy (744-hour obligation period * $5,000/MWh offer cap). While this is a worst-case scenario


       5
           See proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(f)(1)(C).
       6
           See proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(d)(3)(B)(v).

                                                    2 of 24
 example, it is illustrative of the cost risks and procurement limitations presented under the current

availability payment structure in the event ERCOT procures LLDMS on a longer horizon with less

certainty of the system conditions that will occur during that period.

       If ERCOT procures LLDMS on a short- or immediate-term basis—i.e., the week or day(s)

before an anticipated extreme weather condition—ERCOT has no concerns about the PFP’s

proposed availability payment structure. In this scenario, ERCOT will have more information

about actual system conditions and thus will have more certainty as to the procurement need and

quantity. Because the obligation period will be shorter and the amounts procured more closely

aligned to actual deployment needs, the need for and amounts of any availability payments will be

significantly reduced.

       The PFP does not prescribe a long- or short-term procurement model; proposed 16 TAC

§ 25.521(d) instead vests ERCOT with discretion to procure LLDMS on an “as needed” basis.

Consistent with this discretion, ERCOT currently intends to procure LLDMS on a short- or

immediate-term basis, when both the procurement need and quantity are more certain, and thus

does not anticipate an issue with the proposed availability payment structure. However, as

discussed above, the appropriate amount of the availability payment may differ materially if the

service ultimately needs to be procured on a longer-term basis.

       ERCOT accordingly recommends that the Commission avoid establishing a fixed

availability payment percentage in the rule, and instead direct that the appropriate percentage or

amount of any availability payment be determined in the ERCOT Protocols. Allowing this

determination to be made through the ERCOT stakeholder process would provide flexibility to

address and adjust the availability payment as the procurement cadence, participation level and




                                              3 of 24
 needs for this service become better understood. This recommendation is reflected in ERCOT’s

proposed revisions to 16 TAC § 25.521(f)(1)(C) below.

B.     What is an appropriate budget for the LLDMS program?

       ERCOT has no position on the amount of the proposed budget for LLDMS. However,

because ERCOT anticipates using LLDMS chiefly for the winter season, it recommends that the

budget for LLDMS be determined on a 12-month basis, rather than by each calendar year. For

one, if a winter weather event carries over from late December into early January, ERCOT would

need to allocate any LLDMS procurement for such a winter event across two annual budgets, and

would likely need to make separate procurements for the December and January days of the event

to do so. Additionally, if the LLDMS budget year begins on January 1 and ends on December 31,

it is possible that the budget could be exhausted by the winter season and/or by the time of a late

December winter weather event. Setting the LLDMS budget on a 12-month basis avoids these

potential logistical and operational issues.

C.     What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition and how
       far in advance should ERCOT start the auction to procure LLDMS?

       ERCOT already assesses potential and actual extreme weather conditions as a part of its

planning and real-time operations processes. ERCOT believes that those existing long- and short-

term weather forecasting processes are sufficient to assess the risks of and associated with extreme

weather conditions for purposes of procuring and deploying LLDMS.

       The appropriate lead time for initiating the LLDMS procurement depends on the

procurement model used.        If, for example, LLDMS is procured on a monthly basis, the

procurement process could appropriately begin towards the end of the preceding month or earlier.

If, however, LLDMS is procured on a near-term basis, the process could begin once ERCOT has

greater certainty regarding the procurement need and quantity. ERCOT submits that the rule need


                                               4 of 24
 not and should not prescribe specific procurement process timelines.              Proposed 16 TAC

§ 25.521(d)’s directive that LLDMS may be procured on an “as needed” basis provides the

necessary flexibility to accommodate these different procurement scenarios and allows ERCOT to

determine the appropriate timing of procurement under the circumstances based on its risk

assessment and level of certainty regarding the needs for the service.

D.     Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies? If so,
       what limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authority?

       ERCOT recommends against expanding LLDMS to include transmission emergencies at

this time. Unlike extreme weather events, transmission emergencies are typically localized, rather

than system-wide, events. An eligible and qualified large load customer would thus need to be

located in the right place such that their load reduction would result in a reduction for whatever

transmission constraint that led to the transmission emergency.               Introducing locational

procurement with LLDMS would require the development of additional rules and new processes

beyond those needed for the creation of the service. Further, ERCOT does not typically have 24-

hour or other advance notice of transmission emergencies, which makes PURA § 39.170(b)(2)’s

and proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(e)(1)’s 24-hour deployment notice requirement impracticable for

these types of emergencies.

E.     Should large load customers participating in LLDMS be allowed to split their MW
       between LLDMS and some other Ancillary Service or demand response/reliability
       service?

        ERCOT recommends against allowing a large load customer to divide its capacity into

separate components that can be offered into different demand response programs, as this appears

contrary to PURA § 39.170(b)(3) and would be impractical to administer. On the statutory front,

PURA § 39.170(b)(3) “prohibit[s] participation [in LLDMS] by any large load customer . . . that

otherwise participates in a different reliability or ancillary service.” Because this prohibition looks


                                               5 of 24
 to the large load customer as a single unit, the statute appears to foreclose any MW splitting. In

practice, this would only be feasible if the MW offered into each service are metered separately.

Without separate metering, ERCOT would not be able to evaluate each component’s performance.

              II.        COMMENTS ON PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION

        ERCOT offers the following comments and recommendations on the proposed rules for

LLDMS:

A.      Name of the new 16 TAC § 25.521, “Large Load Demand Management Service”

        The PFP adds new rule 16 TAC § 25.521, and titles this new rule “Large Load Demand

Management Service.” Proposed subsection (a)(1) of the rule, however, is unrelated to LLDMS.

This subsection instead concerns Transmission and/or Distribution Service Provider (TDSP)

requirements to ensure large loads can be curtailed during firm load shed, “including the

installation of any necessary equipment or technology before the customer is interconnected.”

ERCOT recommends that the title of 16 TAC § 25.521 be revised to reflect that it governs both

LLDMS and large load curtailment requirements:

        Proposed changes:

        §25.521. Large Load Demand Management Service (LLDMS) and Large
        Load Curtailment Protocols.

B.      16 TAC § 25.521(a), Directives to ERCOT

        1.      Move subsection (a)(1) into a new ending subsection.

        Because proposed subsection (a)(1) concerns a different subject matter than LLDMS,

ERCOT recommends that this proposed language be moved to a new “Large Load Curtailment

Protocols” subsection at the end of the rule. Doing so would help make clear that the curtailment

obligations under this subsection are separate and distinct from the LLDMS requirements and

obligations set forth in the other parts of the rule.



                                                6 of 24
         2.       Clarify subsection (a)(1) as applying only to large load customers.

        Proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(a)(1) applies to “load interconnected after December 31,

2025,” and directs ERCOT to ensure that TDSPs develop protocols to allow “the load to be

curtailed during firm load shed.” ERCOT recommends that this language be clarified to apply

only to new large load customers, rather than all new load. Proposed subsection (a)(1) tracks

PURA § 39.170(a)’s statutory language, which does not explicitly restrict the provision to large

loads. However, the title of PURA § 39.170 references large loads, and that provision was enacted

as a part of S.B. 6, which regulates “large load customers.” 7 The bill’s legislative history also

makes clear that PURA § 39.170(a) was intended to “require[] large load customers served at the

transmission level to install equipment that allows the load to be curtailed during firm load shed.” 8

        To be clear, ERCOT is unaware of any provision that exempts any customer from firm

load-shed, and it has understood that the primary purpose of PURA § 39.170(a) is simply to ensure

that utilities install the appropriate equipment to allow disconnection of large load customers

during a firm load-shed event, given that this was not previously a universal practice. For this

reason, explicitly restricting § 39.170(a)(1) to apply only to large loads would not reasonably

imply an exemption from firm load shed for any other customer.




        7
             See, e.g., PURA § 35.004(c-1) (directing the Commission to ensure that “a large load
customer . . . contributes to the recovery of the interconnecting utility’s costs”) (emphasis added); id. § 37.0561
(“Planning for and Interconnection of Large Loads,” directing the Commission to, inter alia, establish standards for
“interconnecting large load customers in the ERCOT power region”) (emphasis added); id. § 39.169 (“Co-Location
of Large Load Customer with Existing Generation Resource,” governing the co-location of certain “new large load
customers” with certain generation resources) (emphasis added).
          8
               Sen. Research Ctr., Bill Analysis (Enrolled), S.B. 6, 89th Leg., R.S. (2025), available at
https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/analysis/pdf/SB00006F.pdf (further explaining that “stakeholders came together
to identify challenges related to large load growth. S.B. 6 is the culmination of an involved stakeholder process
focused on solving these challenges and ensuring stability for the ERCOT grid.”) (emphasis added).

        Proposed changes:

       (1)    ERCOT must ensure that each electric cooperative, transmission and
              distribution utility, and municipally owned utility serving a transmission-
              voltage customer develops a protocol, including the installation of any
              necessary equipment or technology before the customer is interconnected,
              to allow the a large load customer to be curtailed during firm load shed.
              This subsection applies to a large load customer interconnected after
              December 31, 2025, that is not:

              (A)    load operated by a critical load industrial customer, as defined by
                     Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) §17.002; or

              (B)    designated as a critical natural gas facility under PURA §38.074.

       3.     Strike subsection (a)(2).

       ERCOT also recommends striking the language in proposed subsection (a)(2). Proposed

subsection (i), Implementation, directs ERCOT to “develop, in consultation with commission

staff,” the “additional procedures . . . guides, technical requirements, protocols, or other

standards . . . necessary to develop LLDMS,” which appears to already effect the Legislature’s

directive in PURA § 39.170(b) that the Commission “require [ERCOT] to develop” LLDMS.

       4.     Add new subsection (a), Purpose.

       If the Commission agrees with these recommendations to move proposed subsection (a)(1)

and strike proposed subsection (a)(2), ERCOT recommends the following alternative introductory

provision, which mirrors the language found in 16 TAC § 25.507(a) concerning ERS:

       (a)    Purpose. The purpose of this section is to promote reliability through
              provisions that provide ERCOT flexibility in the implementation and
              administration of the Large Load Demand Management Service (LLDMS).

C.     16 TAC § 25.521(b), Definitions

       1.     Revise definition of “LLDMS obligation period.”

       Proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(b)(3) defines the “LLDMS obligation period” as the period in

which a procured large load customer is obligated to provide LLDMS as “identified in a LLDMS

agreement.”   ERCOT recommends that the obligation period instead be “defined by ERCOT”

                                            8 of 24
 through the utilized procurement mechanism (e.g., request for proposal, auction, request for offers,

etc.) rather than prescribed by a separate agreement. This approach would provide greater

flexibility and avoid the administrative complexity of negotiating and/or executing separate

agreements, which would be particularly difficult or impracticable for short- or immediate-term

procurements.

        Proposed changes:

        (3)        LLDMS obligation period -- The period defined by ERCOT identified in a
                   LLDMS agreement through which a procured large load customer is
                   obligated to provide LLDMS.

        2.         Strike definition of “transmission emergency.”

        As explained in Section I.D above in response to the Commission’s question on

transmission emergencies, ERCOT recommends against expanding LLDMS to include

transmission emergencies because these are generally localized issues that ERCOT has limited to

no advance notice of or ability to forecast. ERCOT thus recommends striking the definition of

transmission emergency from the rule.

D.      16 TAC § 25.521(c), Participation

        1.         Clarify language in subsection (c).

        ERCOT recommends revising proposed subsection 16 TAC § 25.521(c) to clarify that a

large load customer may participate in LLDMS only if it is both pre-qualified and eligible (i.e., not

participating in another Ancillary Service or demand response/reliability service), consistent with

the requirements set forth in proposed subsections (c)(1) (Pre-qualification) and (c)(2)

(Ineligibility).

        Proposed changes:

        (c)        Participation. Participation in LLDMS is limited to eligible large load
                   customers that pre-qualify for participation at least annually.



                                                9 of 24
        2.      Add a provision requiring QSE representation.

       Because ERCOT financially transacts only with Qualified Scheduling Entities (QSEs) and

Congestion Revenue Rights Account Holders, ERCOT recommends adding a new paragraph (3)

under proposed subsection (c)’s “Participation” provisions directing that large load customers

wishing to participate in LLDMS must be represented by a QSE. Other provisions in the proposed

LLDMS rule already implicitly recognize this requirement. For example, proposed subsection

(d)(3) recognizes that offers must be submitted through a QSE; proposed subsection (d)(1) directs

ERCOT to give 24-hour notice of potential deployment to the large load customer’s QSE;

proposed subsection (f)(1) recognizes that LLDMS payments must flow through the QSE; and

proposed subsection (g) allows ERCOT to reduce or claw back payments from the QSE and to

suspend the QSE from participating in the service. ERCOT recommends making this QSE

representation requirement explicit in the rule in the same way that 16 TAC § 25.507(d)(1) does

for ERS.

       Proposed changes:

       (3)     QSE Representation. A large load customer participating in LLDMS must
               be represented by a qualified scheduling entity (QSE).

       3.      Revise subsection (c)(1)(A).

       Proposed subsection (c)(1) prescribes the minimum requirements for a large load customer

to pre-qualify for participation in LLDMS, including that the “large load customer must offer at

least 1 MW of demand reduction.” ERCOT reads this language to impose a restriction on offering

practices, and not prequalification per se. ERCOT recommends revising the language to require

pre-qualification for at least the amount that may be offered and incorporating the 1 MW threshold

into proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(d)(3), which governs LLDMS offer requirements. ERCOT

suggests the following alternative language for subsection (c)(1)(A):



                                              10 of 24
        Proposed changes:

       (1)    Pre-qualification. ERCOT must establish criteria for a large load customer
              to pre-qualify for participation in LLDMS. The criteria for pre-qualification
              must include the following minimum requirements:

              (A)     the large load customer must pre-qualify for at least the amount of
                      demand reduction it plans to offer, which cannot be less than 1 MW
                      offer at least 1 MW of demand reduction; and

              (B)     the large load customer must pass a price responsive test in
                      compliance with ERCOT protocols.

       4.     Clarify language in subsection (c)(2).

       Proposed subsection (c)(2) prohibits large load customers from participating in LLDMS if

they are “participating in the following services or program in the ERCOT market.” ERCOT

understands this proscription to mean that a large load customer may not participate in both

LLDMS and any one or more of the other listed services or programs at the same time, and

accordingly recommends the following clarifying language:

       Proposed changes:

              (2)     Ineligibility. A large load customer participating in any one or more
                      of the following services or program in the ERCOT market during
                      the LLDMS obligation period is not eligible to participate in
                      LLDMS; and a large load customer participating in LLDMS may
                      not participate in any one or more of the following services or
                      program in the ERCOT market during the LLDMS obligation
                      period:

E.     16 TAC § 25.521(d), Procurement

       1.     Revise subsection (d).

       Proposed subsection (d) directs when ERCOT may procure LLDMS—on an “as needed

basis” to “help prevent an anticipated EEA event due to an extreme weather condition or alleviate

an actual EEA event due to an extreme weather condition.” As-written, proposed subsection (d)

could be read as limiting ERCOT’s ability to procure LLDMS until there is an “anticipated” or

“actual” EEA, which implies a level of certainty for procurement (versus deployment) that is not

                                            11 of 24
 required by statute. PURA § 39.170(b) instead appears to more broadly authorize procurement

“to assist with maintaining reliability during extreme weather events.” To avoid ambiguity as to

when ERCOT may procure LLDMS, ERCOT recommends the following revisions, which track

the language in PURA § 39.170(b):

       Proposed changes:

       (d)    Procurement. ERCOT may procure LLDMS from a large load customer
              on an as needed basis to assist with maintaining reliability during extreme
              weather events help prevent an anticipated EEA event due to an extreme
              weather condition or alleviate an actual EEA event due to an extreme
              weather condition.

       2.     Strike subsection (d)(1).

       ERCOT recommends striking proposed subsection (d)(1), which prescribes a specific

LLDMS procurement mechanism (a request for proposal) and four LLDMS procurement

timeframes. As discussed above, the appropriate procurement cadence and procurement

mechanism depends on a number of factors, including the degree of certainty regarding whether

the service will be needed, when the service is needed, the quantity of demand response capacity

needed, and the anticipated obligation period.         The existing “as needed” framework in

subsection (d) provides ERCOT the appropriate flexibility to procure LLDMS based on these and

other considerations, and to allow the procurement model to adjust and evolve with more

experience with this new service.

       3.     Revise subsection (d)(2).

       Proposed subsection (d)(2) directs that, for each LLDMS procurement, the amount of MW

ERCOT procures “must be based on a risk assessment informed by probabilistic modeling.” While

ERCOT uses Monte Carlo probabilistic modeling for certain long-term forecasting activities, those

models look at historical trends and general seasonal weather patterns to predict what system

conditions may look like months or years ahead. ERCOT would not rely on such models for short-

                                            12 of 24
 or near-term LLDMS procurements, and would instead rely on its short-term ensemble load

forecasts, short-term wind and solar forecasts, and other real-time information reflecting expected

system conditions and associated reliability risks. ERCOT therefore recommends the Commission

revise subsection (d)(2) as follows:

       Proposed changes:

       (2)     Quantity. The total quantity of MW that ERCOT procures for an LLDMS
               obligation period must be based on a risk assessment that may be informed
               by probabilistic modeling.

       4.      Revise subsection (d)(3)(A).

       Proposed subsection (d)(3)(A) states that “[a] qualified scheduling entity (QSE) must

submit an offer to ERCOT on behalf of a large load customer that is pre-qualified to participate in

LLDMS.” The emphasized language could be read as requiring QSEs to submit LLDMS offers

to ERCOT; i.e., mandatory LLDMS participation. ERCOT understands that the intent of this

language was instead to direct that, if a qualified and eligible large load customer wishes to

participate in LLDMS, it must submit an offer through a QSE. ERCOT recommends clarifying

this language accordingly.

       Proposed changes:

       (A)     Submission. An eligible and pre-qualified large load customer may submit
               an offer to participate in LLDMS only through its QSE. A qualified
               scheduling entity (QSE) must submit an offer to ERCOT on behalf of a
               large load customer that is pre-qualified to participate in LLDMS. The offer
               must be expressed in dollars per megawatt hour units.

       5.      Revise subsection (d)(3)(B).

       Proposed subsection (d)(3)(B) directs when ERCOT must reject an LLDMS offer. ERCOT

recommends two clarifications to this section: first, ERCOT recommends that the proposed non-

compliance rejection requirement be revised to track the language in proposed subsection (g),

Compliance, which requires ERCOT to establish criteria to suspend a large load customer from


                                              13 of 24
 participating in LLDMS if it fails to comply with its LLDMS obligations. ERCOT understands

that proposed subsection (d)(3)(B)(iii) is intended to prevent ERCOT from accepting offers from

these suspended large load customers, and suggests clarifying that provision accordingly. This

revision also gives ERCOT broader discretion to reject offers from large load customers that have

failed to comply with any of their LLDMS obligations, rather than just a failure to comply with a

prior deployment instruction.

       Second, in line with ERCOT’s recommended changes to subsection (c)(1)(A) above

regarding pre-qualification, ERCOT recommends adding that an LLDMS offer must be rejected if

it exceeds the amount of the large load customer’s pre-qualified demand reduction.

       Proposed changes:

       (B)    Rejection. ERCOT must reject an offer that is:

              (i)     unreasonable;

              (ii)    an outlier when evaluating the parameters of an acceptable offer;

              (iii)   submitted on behalf of a large load customer that ERCOT has
                      suspended from LLDMS participation failed to comply with
                      ERCOT instructions to deploy during the previous LLDMS
                      obligation period;

              (iv)    inconsistent with any other requirement established in ERCOT
                      protocols; or

              (v)     greater than $5,000 per megawatt hour.; or

              (vi)    greater than the amount of the large load customer’s pre-qualified
                      demand reduction, which cannot be less than 1 MW.

F.     16 TAC § 25.521(e), Deployment

       1.     Clarify language in subsections (e)(1), (2) and (3).

       Each of the proposed LLDMS deployment provisions, subsections (e)(1), (2) and (3), refer

generally to ERCOT’s deployment of “large load customers.” ERCOT recommends that this



                                            14 of 24
 language be revised to make clear that the large load customer that may be deployed under these

sections are “large load customer[s] participating in LLDMS.”

        Proposed changes:

       (1)     Prior to deployment, ERCOT must provide at least 24-hour notice to a QSE
               that a large load customer participating in LLDMS represented by the QSE
               may be deployed to reduce its load during the LLDMS obligation period.

       (2)     ERCOT may deploy a large load customer participating in LLDMS as
               necessary to help maintain reliability during an EEA event due to an
               extreme weather condition throughout the LLDMS obligation period.

       (3)     When deployed by ERCOT, a large load customer participating in LLDMS
               must deploy consistent with its obligations and must remain deployed:

                      (A)     for the duration of the EEA event; or

                      (B)     until the large load customer can be recalled safely, as
                              determined and communicated by ERCOT

       2.      Revise subsection (e)(2).

       Proposed subsection (e)(2) governs when ERCOT may deploy LLDMS large load

customers. In relevant part, this provision directs that ERCOT may deploy these loads when

“necessary to help maintain reliability during an EEA event due to an extreme weather condition

throughout the LLDMS obligation period.” The emphasized language appears to prohibit ERCOT

from deploying LLDMS large loads unless and until it has declared EEA; however,

PURA § 39.170(b) calls for the deployment of these loads “in the event of an anticipated

emergency condition.” ERCOT thus recommends revising subsection (e)(2) to allow for LLDMS

deployment both when there is an actual and anticipated EEA.

       ERCOT also recommends removing the language “throughout the LLDMS obligation

period” at the end of this provision, which could be read as qualifying “extreme weather condition”

and limiting ERCOT’s deployment ability to extreme weather conditions that span the entirety of

the LLDMS obligation period. ERCOT understands this language is intended qualify which types


                                             15 of 24
 of large loads may be deployed (those with LLDMS obligations) and for how long (consistent with

their LLDMS obligations), but both these points are already addressed by adding “participating in

LLDMS” to this provision as suggested above and by the next subsection (e)(3).

       Proposed changes:

       (2)     ERCOT may deploy a large load customer participating in LLDMS as
               necessary to help maintain reliability in anticipation of and during an EEA
               event due to an extreme weather condition throughout the LLDMS
               obligation period.

       3.      Revise subsection (e)(3) to address EEA events that extend beyond the LLDMS
               obligation period.

       Proposed subsection (e)(3) generally addresses a LLDMS large load customer’s

deployment obligations once instructed by ERCOT to deploy. Namely, the large load customer

must “deploy consistent with its obligations” and must remain deployed for either the duration of

the EEA event or until it can be safely recalled. To avoid any dispute about whether the phrase

“consistent with its obligations” might imply that the customer is not required to remain deployed

beyond the EEA event, ERCOT recommends further revising subsection (e)(3) to clarify that

deployed LLDMS loads must remain deployed for the duration of the EEA event, even if the EEA

event extends beyond the LLDMS obligation period.

        Proposed changes:

       (3)     When deployed by ERCOT, a large load customer participating in LLDMS
               must deploy consistent with its obligations and, notwithstanding the length
               of the LLDMS obligation period, must remain deployed:

               (A)    for the duration of the EEA event; or

               (B)    until the large load customer can be recalled safely, as determined
                      and communicated by ERCOT.




                                            16 of 24
 G.        16 TAC § 25.521(f), Payment and Charges

     1.         Revise subsection (f)(1)(C).

          For the reasons explained in Section I.A above with respect to the Commission’s question

on availability payments, ERCOT recommends that the Commission avoid establishing a fixed

B.     What is an appropriate budget for the LLDMS program?

       ERCOT has no position on the amount of the proposed budget for LLDMS. However,

because ERCOT anticipates using LLDMS chiefly for the winter season, it recommends that the

budget for LLDMS be determined on a 12-month basis, rather than by each calendar year. For

one, if a winter weather event carries over from late December into early January, ERCOT would

need to allocate any LLDMS procurement for such a winter event across two annual budgets, and

would likely need to make separate procurements for the December and January days of the event

potential logistical and operational issues.

planning and real-time operations processes. ERCOT believes that those existing long- and short-

term weather forecasting processes are sufficient to assess the risks of and associated with extreme

weather conditions for purposes of procuring and deploying LLDMS.

procurement model used.        If, for example, LLDMS is procured on a monthly basis, the

procurement process could appropriately begin towards the end of the preceding month or earlier.

D.     Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies? If so,
       what limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authority?

       ERCOT recommends against expanding LLDMS to include transmission emergencies at

this time. Unlike extreme weather events, transmission emergencies are typically localized, rather

than system-wide, events. An eligible and qualified large load customer would thus need to be

located in the right place such that their load reduction would result in a reduction for whatever

transmission constraint that led to the transmission emergency.               Introducing locational

procurement with LLDMS would require the development of additional rules and new processes

beyond those needed for the creation of the service. Further, ERCOT does not typically have 24-

hour or other advance notice of transmission emergencies, which makes PURA § 39.170(b)(2)' s

and proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(e)(1)'s 24-hour deployment notice requirement impracticable for

these types of emergencies.
